html: 1.1 What Is Science?
Look around you right now. Something is happening everywhere you turn.

A fan is spinning. Sunlight is falling through a window and landing in a bright patch on the floor. Somewhere nearby, water is boiling, or a bird is calling, or dust is drifting through a beam of light. None of this is unusual. All of it is worth a second look.

You have been noticing things like this your whole life — why the moon seems to follow the car, why ice feels wet, why your shadow stretches long in the evening. Those questions were not childish. They were the beginning of something.
Now you are ready to go further.
An ordinary event can become a scientific question when you look closely.

Science is not a pile of facts to memorise. Science is a way of working. It means observing carefully, asking sharp questions, testing what you think you know, and being willing to change your mind when the evidence says you should.
Science Is Not Kept in a Building
Science does not live in laboratories. Laboratories are useful, but science is wherever something is happening.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="154" height="156" viewBox="748 95 290 292" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 411.7862072933132, "y": 165.02062688087062, "w": 558.6482997001056, "h": 793.3656326944706}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-2"><rect x="748" y="95" width="290" height="292"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-2)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p002-reference.png" x="0" y="0" width="1052" height="1494"><title>A dosa cooking in a pan.</title></image></svg>

html: It is in the kitchen, where heat turns a soft batter into a firm, holey dosa. It is on the cricket field, where a ball bends in the air because of the way it was spun. It is in the soil under a mango tree, where organisms too small to see are breaking down fallen leaves. It is inside your own body, where your heart is beating right now without being told to.
An Unfinished Map
Here is something surprising: science is not finished.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="154" height="156" viewBox="715 474 326 307" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 471.2392365280269, "y": 280.5736094856675, "w": 496.9570700785786, "h": 705.7547392239412}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-3"><polygon points="810,474 1041,474 1041,781 950,781 715,720 715,705"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-3)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p002-reference.png" x="0" y="0" width="1052" height="1494"><title>An unfinished map and pencil.</title></image></svg>

html: Think of what we know as a map of a huge, mostly unexplored land. Some regions are surveyed in fine detail. Others are sketched roughly. Some are still blank. And every time explorers map a new region, its edges open onto territory nobody knew existed. The map does not shrink the unknown — it reveals more of it.

Sometimes the mapmakers get it wrong. For centuries people were certain the Sun travelled around the Earth, because that is exactly what it looks like. Careful observation showed otherwise, and the map had to be redrawn. That correction was not a failure of science. It was science working as it should.
The Most Important Tool
You will use many instruments in this book — thermometers, magnets, lenses, balances. But the tool that matters most is not one you can hold. It is curiosity.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="154" height="156" viewBox="757 917 278 289" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 402.34599042085904, "y": 423.01034502576226, "w": 567.8616403566435, "h": 806.4498465380582}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-4"><rect x="757" y="917" width="278" height="289"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-4)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p002-reference.png" x="0" y="0" width="1052" height="1494"><title>An open flower and a closed bud.</title></image></svg>

html: Curiosity is what makes you look up at a night sky and wonder what the stars actually are, and how far away. It is what makes you notice that a flower on your balcony is shut at dawn and open by mid-morning, and then wonder how it knows.

blocks.html: Why might this happen? A flower has no eyes and no clock. What could it be responding to? You do not need the right answer yet — only a reasonable guess. A possible explanation is a hypothesis. A prediction states what you expect to observe if it is right. For example, if light triggers opening, what should happen when the plant is shaded?

html: One Idea in Many Places

Some of what you learn in this book will be useful the same week you learn it. You will understand why food spoils faster in May than in December, why a frayed electrical wire is dangerous, how boiling kills many disease-causing microbes in water, while leaving dissolved chemical contaminants behind.
But the real reward comes later, and it is stranger than that.

Leave a wet shirt on a line and by evening it is dry. Pour water into an earthen matka and the water inside stays cool even on a hot afternoon. Watch the sky before the monsoon and see clouds thickening where there was clear blue an hour ago.
Three ordinary things. They seem to have nothing to do with each other.
Two involve evaporation directly; cloud formation needs another change as well.

html: In all three, water is leaving a liquid surface and moving into the air as an invisible vapour. That is what dries the shirt. That is what cools the matka — water seeping through the clay escapes from its surface and carries warmth away with it. Evaporation supplies water vapour. Clouds become visible when vapour cools and condenses into droplets or forms ice crystals; vapour itself is invisible.

blocks.html: Can you explain why? If evaporation cools the matka, what does that suggest about why you feel cold when you step out of a swimming pool into the wind?

html: Evaporation connects the shirt and the pot. Cloud formation also requires condensation or ice formation. Name each change rather than treating every water process as the same event.
Clouds become visible when cooling water vapour condenses into tiny droplets or forms ice crystals. Evaporation supplies the vapour; condensation helps form clouds.
A shared explanation can connect observations; check where it works and where another process is needed.
1.2 What This Book Will Ask You
Begin with the Earth — as far as we know, the only place in the universe where anything is alive.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="874" height="170" viewBox="30 1080 994 270" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 194.1851746787321, "y": -455.99998052633964, "w": 662.3703258465817, "h": 941.296476027449}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-8"><rect x="30" y="1080" width="994" height="270"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-8)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p003-reference.png" x="0" y="0" width="1052" height="1495"><title>A seedling, food, water, everyday materials and the Moon.</title></image></svg>

html: A seed pushes a pale shoot up through dark soil. A caterpillar seals itself away and comes out with wings. A calf that could barely stand in the morning is running across the field by the end of the month. Growing is so ordinary that we stop noticing it happening. But how does a plant build an entire body out of soil, water and air?

Living things need materials and energy to grow. Green plants make sugars using light, water and carbon dioxide; animals obtain food by eating. In a country this large, that alone is a huge subject — pongal in one state, litti in another, a fish curry along the coast, a plate of rajma somewhere north. What are these dishes actually made of? And how could you find out for yourself, instead of being told?

Then there is water. You have jumped into a puddle after rain. But where was that water an hour before it fell on you, and how did it get up there? Cool it and it turns to ice. Heat it and it leaves as steam. What is going on?
And how hot is hot? When someone in your house has a fever, nobody wants a guess. They want a number.

Now look at what things are made of — paper, the metal of a key, a plastic scale, a rubber eraser, the magnet holding a cupboard shut, the cloth of your shirt. Each one was chosen for a reason. Could a key be made of rubber? Why not?
And when the Earth runs out of questions, there is the sky above it.

These questions connect different parts of science. Following water leads from a puddle to the weather. Studying a plant leads to light, air and food. Comparing materials leads to the design of useful objects. Look for these connections as you read. Ask what changes something, and what evidence could help explain it.
Every one of these has an answer. Not all of them are in this book.

blocks.html: You already do science. You have simply never called it that.
Suppose the clock on your wall has stopped. Both hands are frozen at ten past four.
The first thing you do is ask a question, even if only in your head: why has it stopped?

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="874" height="295" viewBox="80 1045 925 350" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 68.7499980407598, "y": -597.7857503153782, "w": 886.685645015123, "h": 1260.0715818501685}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-9"><rect x="80" y="1045" width="925" height="350"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-9)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p005-reference.png" x="0" y="0" width="1052" height="1495"><title>Clock hands touching and a replacement cell.</title></image><rect class="food-white" x="603" y="1087" width="147" height="28"/><rect class="food-white" x="831" y="1090" width="47" height="28"/><text class="se-caption se-bold" x="608" y="1109">Hands touching</text><text class="se-caption se-bold" x="837" y="1112">Cell</text></svg>

blocks.html: Then, almost without noticing, you make a guess. The cell inside must be finished.
Making a guess is the easy part. What matters is what you do next. You take the clock down, open the back, and fit a new cell.
If the hands begin to move, a used-up cell is one explanation. Refitting the cell also changed its contact with the terminals, so that observation alone does not prove which change mattered.
But suppose they do not move.

Now stop and notice something. The clock is still stopped, so it feels as though nothing has been achieved. That is not true. A failed replacement narrows the possibilities only if the new cell works, faces the right way and makes contact. Check these before ruling out the cell as a cause.
So you make a second guess. Perhaps the cell is fine but is not pressing properly against the metal contacts. You push it in firmly and give it a moment. Still nothing.
A third guess, then: something inside is stuck. You look more closely and find the thin second hand has caught against the minute hand and cannot pass it.
Question. Guess. Test. Look honestly at what happened. Guess again if you must.
Nobody sat you down and taught you that sequence. Yet it is very close to what a scientist does when facing something no one has ever explained.

html: The Steps Behind It
What you did with the clock has a name. It is called the scientific method, and written out plainly it looks like this:
1. Observe something that puzzles you or catches your interest.
2. Ask a question about it.
3. Guess a possible answer.
4. Test the guess, through an experiment or through further careful observation.
5. Examine the result and decide whether it actually answers your question.

That list looks tidier than real life ever is. Very often you finish step five only to discover you are back at step three with a fresh guess. Sometimes the test throws up something you were not even looking for, and that becomes a better question than the one you started with.

This is one useful route through an investigation, not a compulsory order for every kind of science. What matters is that the guess comes before the test, and that you accept the result even when it is not the one you wanted.
An observation describes what you notice: the clock hands have not moved. An explanation suggests a reason: the cell may be used up. Keeping these separate helps you test your idea honestly.

For a fair comparison, change one thing while keeping other conditions similar. If you replace the cell and free the hands together, you will not know which change mattered. Repeating a check can help you spot a result that happened only by chance.

blocks.html: Write about a problem you worked out for yourself recently. It does not have to be a science problem. List the steps you took, in order. Was there a point where you had to change your first guess?

html: Everyone Does This
Scientists follow the scientific method for a living. But nobody owns it, and it is used every day by people who would never call themselves scientists.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="186" height="133" viewBox="0 0 680 724" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 807.5414289059413, "y": 214.00000189986895, "w": 398.9999380167644, "h": 132.99979956379138}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-10"><rect x="0" y="0" width="680" height="724"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-10)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p007-everyday-science.png" x="0" y="0" width="2172" height="724"><title>Cook inspecting batter</title></image></svg>

html: A cook lifts the lid off the idli batter in the morning and finds it flat instead of risen. She asks why. Was the kitchen too cold overnight? Was the batter ground too thin? She will not solve it by worrying — she will change one thing tomorrow and watch what happens.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="186" height="133" viewBox="690 0 758 724" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 673.6229334765518, "y": 383.0001310909811, "w": 398.9999829605473, "h": 132.99979956378957}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-11"><rect x="690" y="0" width="758" height="724"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-11)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p007-everyday-science.png" x="0" y="0" width="2172" height="724"><title>Tailor checking a needle</title></image></svg>

html: A tailor's machine starts skipping stitches. He does not replace the whole machine. He checks the needle first, then the thread tension, then the bobbin — one at a time, because changing everything at once would tell him nothing.

art.svg: <svg class="science-illustration" width="186" height="133" viewBox="1448 0 724 724" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet" overflow="hidden" data-original-bounds="{"x": 537.4999904412826, "y": 528.9998299616982, "w": 398.9999829605473, "h": 132.99979956379138}"><defs><clipPath id="se-art-clip-12"><rect x="1448" y="0" width="724" height="724"/></clipPath></defs><image clip-path="url(#se-art-clip-12)" href="../../figures/class-6/science/ch01-p007-everyday-science.png" x="0" y="0" width="2172" height="724"><title>Electrician checking a disconnected fitting</title></image></svg>

html: An electrician is called about a tubelight that flickers for a long time before it steadies. Is it the tube, the starter, or the wiring? Each of those can be tested separately.

None of them are in a laboratory. All of them are doing exactly what step three and step four describe: guess, then test — and crucially, test one thing at a time, so that the result actually means something.

A useful record is specific. Describe which part of a puddle’s edge moved and when. A sketch can preserve details that memory loses. Keep what you observed separate from your explanation of why it happened.

blocks.html: Choose one thing near your home that changes over time — a plant on a windowsill, a puddle after rain, ants around a spill, the shadow of a pole.
Watch it for five minutes without doing anything to it.
Write down three things you actually saw. Not what you think should happen — what happened.
Write one question your observation raised.

html: 1.4 Curiosity, Company and a Long Road
Everything in this chapter rests on one habit, and it is not a difficult one. Notice things.

Noticing sounds too simple to matter. It is not. Most people walk past a hundred small oddities a day without registering a single one. The person who stops and says hold on, that's strange has done the hardest part already. Everything else — the questions, the guesses, the tests — follows from that pause.

And you do not have to do any of it alone. Science has a reputation for lonely geniuses, and it is mostly wrong. Discoveries today come from teams, often spread across many countries, arguing with one another and checking each other's work. Being told you are wrong by someone who has looked carefully at your evidence is not an insult. It is one of the most useful things that can happen to you.
So when you are stuck, ask someone. Compare what you saw with what your friend saw. If you disagree about what happened, that disagreement is worth more than either of your answers.

One last thing, and it is important. You will not find the answers to all your questions this year. Some of what you wonder about in Grade 6 you will only understand in Grade 9, or later, or possibly never — because nobody has worked it out yet.
That is not a warning. It is the best part.

Describe an event separately from a friend, then compare your accounts. Did you notice the same details? Which statements describe what you saw, and which suggest a reason? Differences give you something to check together. Finding an answer may need longer observation, a better comparison, or a more precise question.

blocks.html: Write down one "Why?" question about something you have noticed but never had explained. How might you begin to find the answer? Who could you ask, and what could you test?

html: Science begins with noticing. It continues with asking. And it never quite ends.
